author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A federal judge in Boston on Friday blocked the government from continuing to ask applicants for career civil-service jobs to write essays explaining how they would help advance the president’s policies and executive orders. U.S. District Judge George O’Toole issued the ruling in a case brought by three unions representing public employees.

O’Toole concluded that the unions were likely to show the question infringed applicants’ speech rights and violated the Administrative Procedure Act. His decision noted that federal civil-service law bars hiring decisions based on political affiliation. The unions said more than 70,000 job postings had included the question, covering positions as varied as air traffic control specialist, crane operator and nuclear materials courier.

The Office of Personnel Management did not immediately comment on the ruling. The agency previously said the response was optional and that political beliefs could not be used in hiring decisions. The question was adopted as part of a hiring plan developed after a January 2025 executive order. The order halts the essay requirement while the unions’ challenge proceeds.
dek: U.S. District Judge George O’Toole halted a question asking civil-service applicants how they would advance presidential policies and executive orders.
headline: Boston judge blocks federal hiring essay question
